USA.rationale:
RECOMMENDATION: Continue active negotiations with China toward a comprehensive deal within the next four weeks. Do not escalate tariffs or add new entity-list measures — the current leverage is sufficient and escalation risks spooking markets and allies. Do not concede on enforcement mechanisms or tariff-removal timing prematurely. Hold firm on structural IP/tech-transfer demands while remaining at the table.

SUPPORTING RATIONALE: The US holds a moderate structural advantage (threat_score = -0.3). China's economy is significantly weaker than the US: industrial output growth fell to a 17-year low of 5.3% in Jan-Feb 2019 (Reuters, Mar 14), manufacturing PMI contracted in Feb 2019 for the first time since 2009, industrial profits fell 14% YoY in Jan-Feb, and the jobless rate spiked to 5.3%. Meanwhile, the US economy is slowing but resilient — Q1 2019 GDP tracking at 2.1-2.5%, S&P 500 posted its best Q1 since 1998, and the Fed has shifted to a patient/dovish stance at 2.42%. The trade deficit narrowed in Feb 2019, improving the GDP outlook. This asymmetry gives the US leverage: China needs a deal more than the US does.

On the dispute itself, the tariff war has reached ~$250B in US coverage with matching Chinese retaliation. The Huawei/5G campaign is partially effective — Australia, Japan, New Zealand have restricted Huawei, but Britain, Germany, and India are resisting a full ban (NYT, Mar 18). The DOJ has unsealed criminal charges against Huawei. Talks as of April 3-4 showed progress on text including enforcement language, but two critical sticking points remain: (1) enforcement mechanism — China wants all tariffs removed, US wants to keep tariffs as leverage; (2) structural issues (IP theft, forced tech transfer) have no agreed timeline. Trump said 'we'll know over the next four weeks' — the window is open but not indefinite.

Action_score at -0.05 reflects a 'negotiate with slight edge' posture. The US should stay at the table with leverage intact. Escalation now (adding List 4 tariffs or broadening Huawei restrictions) would be counterproductive: it could derail talks when a deal is close, trigger further market volatility, and fracture allied unity on Huawei. Concession now (rolling back tariffs) would squander leverage when China's economy is weakening. The correct play is patience — maintain current tariff levels, push hard on enforcement, and give negotiators the four weeks Trump referenced.
key_factors: China industrial output at 17-year low (5.3% YoY Jan-Feb 2019)
US economy resilient: Q1 tracking 2.1-2.5%, S&P best Q1 since 1998
Two sticking points: enforcement mechanism and tariff removal timing
Huawei campaign partially effective but allies resisting full ban
Talks showing progress — April 3-4 round reported progress on enforcement text
Fed shifted to patient/dovish, removing domestic economic pressure
China's manufacturing PMI contracted Feb 2019, industrial profits fell 14%

sources_cited.excerpt: Intensive Washington talks between US and Chinese negotiators; both sides report progress on text, including enforcement language. No final deal signed.
The two sides still disagree over whether the US will use tariffs as an enforcement tool. Trump has said tariffs on $250B could stay in place even after a deal. China wants removal.
Growth in China's industrial output fell to a 17-year low in the first two months of the year and the jobless rate rose, pointing to further weakness in the world's second-biggest economy.
Britain, Germany, India and UAE signaling they are unlikely to back the American effort to entirely ban Huawei from building their 5G networks.
JPMorgan raised Q1 GDP forecast to about 2.5% annualized. Goldman Sachs boosted tracking estimate to 2.1%. GDPNow at 2.4%.
10-year Treasury yield fell from 3.2% (Nov 2018) to 2.53% (Apr 24, 2019), a -0.55 percentage point decline signaling growth concerns but also Fed dovishness.
